title: Unavailable, Unethical, Unhinged: U.S. H-bomb Unit in Germany Should be First to Go
author: John Laforge
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screen-
Shot-2026-07-29-at-2.10.56-PM-680x398.png)

Anti-nuclear activists placed sunflowers, a symbol of nuclear disarmament, in
the fence at Germany's Büchel air base Thur., July 24, marking the 30th
anniversary of protests at the base. Photo by Luthar Lange.

For the last four years, the U.S. hydrogen bombs stationed in Germany have
been stranded at Büchel Air Force Base, southeast of Cologne, unavailable to
the fighter jets and pilots that are rehearsed and ready to detonate them
against Russia. These WMD have been unusable for nuclear attacks or threats —
i.e. ‘deterrence’ — since 2022 because the base is getting a makeover.

The deterrence that the U.S. and Germany say the nuclear weapons provide
disappeared in 2022 when massive remodeling of the base began. A total rebuild
of its runway and more forced the base’s 46 Tornado fighter jets to be moved
to Nörvenich Air Base, 28 miles away, to practice their take-offs, attacks,
and landings.

Because the base’s reconstruction has left the ‘nuclear deterrent’ unavailable
for years, the unoccupied and redundant U.S. Air Force’s 702d Munitions
Support Squadron (or MUNSS) should be the first unit withdrawn from Germany
under Trump’s recent orders.

The Department of War says the 702d MUNSS is needed because it ‘receives,
stores, maintains, controls, and employs war reserve munitions in support of
[Büchel’s] 33rd Tactical Air Wing’s role in NATO’s strike mission.’ This, of
course, has been mission impossible for at least four years, a pause that
means relief from the self-destructive threat of nuclear strike missions aimed
at Russia.

The ‘Commander’s Welcome Letter’ for new arrivals, on Büchel’s website,
explains: ‘The 702d consists of approximately 170 personnel across 26
different Air Force Specialties, responsible for maintaining, operating, and
securing $6B [billion] in Protection Level-1 assets….’ And according to a Shaw
Air Force Base manual, ‘Protection Level 1’ resources ‘include nuclear weapons
and … systems critical to the success of active nuclear missions….’

Büchel’s nuclear mission involves twenty U.S. B61 H-bombs — the only remaining
nuclear weapons in Germany — which are polished on base by the 702d MUNSS.
This arsenal is the crux of a so-called ‘nuclear sharing’ arrangement between
the United States and Germany (and four other NATO countries). But neither
‘active nuclear missions’ nor any other kind have flown out of Büchel since
2022, leaving the 702d on holiday.

Declaring he would reduce Germany’s U.S. military presence, Trump said May 2,
“We are going to cut way down, and we’re cutting a lot further than 5,000.”
Liana Fix reported for the Council on Foreign Relations that 5,000 troops were
about one-seventh of the roughly 38,000 GIs currently stationed in
Deutschland. Secretary Hegseth promptly had the Pentagon claim that the
decision on withdrawals had followed a ‘thorough review of the force posture
in Europe.’

The actual fatuous reason for the potential drawdown was a Trump tantrum over
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s derisive public assessment that the U.S.
was being ‘humiliated’ by Iran. Merz said to students last April, ‘[T]he
Iranians are … letting the Americans travel to Islamabad and then leave again
without any result. An entire nation is being humiliated by the Iranian
leadership’, The Guardian reported. Trump’s reactionary fit opens a door to
the long-sought-after removal of U.S. nuclear weapons from Germany, something
that the Parliament/Bundestag — moved by mass public pressure — formally
instructed the government to pursue in March 2010.

For decades, Tactical Air Force Wing 33 has reportedly been operating 46
Tornado jet fighters. The Tornados are flown by German pilots who train to
carry the U.S. H-bombs and to detonate them against Russia if a U.S. president
so orders. While the Tornados returned to Büchel this year, the first F-35s
are set to replace them starting in 2027.

Indeed, the two billion Euros being spent on the Büchel rebuild (widening
taxiways and airfield intersections; new runway; new cargo apron; and a new
so-called fighter jet ‘campus’), is in preparation for the delivery of new
U.S. ‘B61-model 12’ thermonuclear bombs, and the arrival of new F-35A fighter-
jets to carry them.

The F-35s from Lockheed Martin cost Germany over ten billion euros, or $11.4
billion, according to Aero.de, Dec. 12, 2022. And Aero reported June 24, 2025,
that the F-35s are ‘intended to support Germany’s so-called “nuclear sharing”
program — a NATO deterrence strategy under which allies have access to U.S.
nuclear weapons in the event of war.’

If there is any seriousness to Trump’s erratic outburst about troop
withdrawals from Germany, nothing could be more reassuring, more stabilizing,
and more de-escalatory than throwing out the 702d MUNSS along with its nuclear
suicide mission.
